meta.blurb: An inventor builds a machine that can travel through time, then returns pale, bruised and silent. His story takes us to the year 802,701, where gentle people play in the sun and something terrible waits underground. What happened to the world we know?
meta.bible: Time Traveller: an inventor and scientist from Victorian England, curious, brave and never named. Narrator: a guest at the dinners who writes the story down. Filby: a lively, argumentative guest. Psychologist: a guest who doubts the idea. Medical Man: a guest. Mayor: a Provincial Mayor, a guest. Richmond: the town near London where the Time Traveller lives. London: the city. Time Machine: a small machine of ivory, brass and crystal with two Levers. Fourth Dimension: Time, in the Time Traveller's talk. Year 802,701: the year in which the Time Traveller lands. Sphinx: a white stone statue on a bronze Pedestal, with secret doors. Eloi: small, gentle, beautiful, childlike people who live above ground in the sun, and eat only fruit. Morlocks: pale, apelike people with big eyes who live underground in the dark and work machines. Weena: a small Eloi woman whom the Time Traveller saves from a river. Wells: deep shafts down into the underworld. Palace of Green Porcelain: a ruined museum made of green china. Matches and Camphor: the things he takes from the Palace. Iron bar: his weapon. Thames: the river near the Eloi. Hill: the green hill where he sleeps. Crabs: huge sea creatures on the shore of the far future. Last beach: the end of the world, a red sun, ice and darkness. Voice and tone: serious and curious, told by a man at a dinner table; dangers are real but never gory; the ending leaves the reader thinking, with one small thread of hope: two white flowers.

A1A2: Some friends came to dinner at the Time Traveller's house in Richmond.
The Time Traveller said that time is a fourth dimension, like length and height.
His friends laughed and said, “You cannot travel in time!”
He showed them a tiny machine, and it slowly disappeared from the table.
Then he showed them a bigger machine that he was making in his laboratory.
The next Thursday, the friends sat down to dinner, but he did not come.
At last he came in, dirty, tired and pale, and his foot was hurt.
After he ate, he said, “Listen, and I will tell you everything.”
He sat on the machine and pulled a lever, and he felt very strange.
Day and night came faster and faster, and the sun was a bright line.
He stopped the machine, fell on the grass and heard hail all around him.
Through the storm, he saw a huge white statue with wings, called a sphinx.
Small, beautiful people came running out of the rain and stood around him.
They spoke softly, gave him flowers and laughed when he pointed at the sky.
He looked for his machine, but it was not there anymore.
He stayed with the little people and slowly learned some of their words.
They ate only fruit, lived in big houses and slept all together.
“Maybe people became too comfortable,” he thought, “and now nobody needs to work.”
One day a small woman fell into a river, and he saved her.
Her name was Weena, and she became his friend and followed him everywhere.
At night, he saw white shapes in the dark, and the little people were afraid.
He found deep wells in the ground and heard machines working far below.
He thought, “Some other kind of people must live under the ground.”
He climbed down a well and saw strange, pale creatures in the dark.
They tried to catch him, but he escaped and climbed up again.
He learned that these creatures, the Morlocks, took people from above for food.
He thought that rich people and poor people had slowly become two kinds of creatures.
He understood that the Morlocks had taken his machine inside the white sphinx.
He took Weena and walked to a big green palace to find a weapon.
In the old palace, he found matches, camphor and a strong iron bar.
At night, in a dark wood, Weena was too tired to walk.
He lit a fire to keep the Morlocks away, but the dry trees burned.
There was smoke everywhere, and in the fight he lost Weena for ever.
At dawn, he sat in the ashes, alone and very sad.
He went back to the sphinx, and now its bronze doors were open.
He walked in, found his machine, and then the doors closed behind him.
The Morlocks reached for him, but he pulled the lever and escaped.
Millions of years later, he saw a huge red sun and giant crabs.
At the end of the world, it was dark and cold, and almost nothing lived.
He turned the machine around and came back to his own laboratory.
He finished his story, and his friends sat and looked at him.
They did not believe him, and the Time Traveller had no proof.
The next day, the narrator went to the laboratory and found him packing.
“I will be back soon,” he said, and he showed two strange white flowers.
The narrator waited for a long time, but the Time Traveller never came back.
Three years passed, and there was still no news.
The narrator asked himself if this could really be our future.
He also thought that people could still make a better world.
He kept the two white flowers to remember Weena.
He thought that kindness could live on, even in a dark future.
B1B2: One evening, a group of friends gather for dinner at the house of the Time Traveller in Richmond. Their host has not come down yet, so they sit by the fire and wait for him.
When he arrives, he asks them to think about the world in a new way. Everything has length, width and height, he says, but it also lasts for a length of time, and time is a fourth dimension.
The Psychologist and Filby think that this is nonsense, and they say that nobody can move through time. The Time Traveller smiles, because he is sure that he can prove them wrong.
He puts a small, shining model of his machine on the table and pushes a tiny lever. The model grows faint and then disappears, and the guests stare at the empty table in silence.
Afterward, he leads some of them down to his laboratory, where a larger machine of ivory, brass and crystal stands half finished. He says that it will carry a man into the past or the future.
The following Thursday, the guests return for dinner, but the Time Traveller is not there. After a while they decide to start without him, and they leave an empty chair at the head of the table.
At last the door opens, and their host limps in, pale and dirty, with his coat torn and his hair full of dust. He says that he must wash and eat first, and then he will explain.
When he is rested and fed, he settles in his chair and begins. He tells them that he finished the machine that very morning and could not wait a moment longer to try it.
As soon as he pulls the lever, he feels dizzy and sick, as if he were falling. Day and night begin to flash past him, faster and faster, like the wings of a black bird.
The sun becomes a bright streak across the sky, and the walls of his laboratory melt away. Buildings rise and fall around him like bubbles, and he is so frightened that he pulls the lever back.
The machine stops suddenly and throws him onto soft grass, and a sharp hailstorm beats on his head. He gets up, wet and shaking, and looks around at a strange, hilly country.
Through the gray rain, he sees a huge white statue standing on a bronze base. It is a sphinx, with the face of a person and wings that seem to be made of stone.

Soon, small people in bright robes come out of the rain and gather around him. They are only about four feet tall, with soft hair and graceful faces, and they are the most beautiful people he has ever seen.
They speak to him in soft voices and put flowers around his neck as if they had been waiting for him. When he points up at the sky to show where he comes from, they only laugh.
The Time Traveller walks back to where he left his machine, but nothing is there except the marks of its feet in the grass. His heart sinks, because without the machine he cannot get home.

He decides to stay with the little people and tries to learn from them, but at first he understands very little. Slowly, by pointing at things and repeating words, he learns enough to ask simple questions.
He sees that they live in huge, ruined halls and eat nothing but fruit. At night they all sleep together in large rooms, close to one another, as though they are afraid of something.
He sees that they tire easily and seem to care about nothing very much. At first, he thinks that mankind has grown weak in a world where there is no need to work.
One afternoon, a small woman falls into the river and begins to drown, and nobody comes to help her. The Time Traveller jumps in and pulls her out, and the little people only stand and watch.
The woman, whose name is Weena, is grateful, and she follows him everywhere afterward and gives him flowers. She is as gentle as a child, and he begins to feel real affection for her.
At night, the Time Traveller sees pale shapes moving in the dark, and the Eloi cry out in fear. He knows then that these gentle people are not as safe as they seem.
Walking the countryside, he finds round wells with no water in them, and from deep inside he hears the beating of great machines. A warm wind blows up from the dark, and he cannot see the bottom.

He starts to think that the beautiful little people live on the surface because something else lives below. Perhaps the machines that keep their world running are cared for by creatures who never see the sun.
With a heavy heart, he climbs down one of the wells by small metal rungs. At the bottom, in the faint light of his last matches, he sees pale, apelike creatures with huge eyes that shine in the dark.
The creatures, called Morlocks, grab at him, and he is very afraid. He strikes a match and climbs up as fast as he can, and the light keeps them back until he reaches the surface.
Gradually, he understands why the Eloi are afraid of the dark. At night, the Morlocks come up from below, and they carry away Eloi to eat them.

He now believes that, long ago, the rich and the poor drifted apart until they became two different kinds of people. One kind lives above in the sun and does nothing, and the other works in darkness and now feeds on its masters.
Then he realizes that the Morlocks have taken his machine, because the marks of its feet lead to the sphinx. The bronze doors in its base are shut tight, and the Morlocks must have hidden it inside.

He knows that he will need a weapon and a good light if he is to fight the Morlocks. He remembers a huge ruined building in the distance, called the Palace of Green Porcelain, and he sets out toward it with Weena.
The palace is a vast, dusty museum full of rusty machines and broken glass cases. In the gloom, he finds a box of matches, a lump of camphor and a strong iron bar, and he takes all three.
As the sun begins to sink, the pair set off through a thick forest on the way home. Weena is so tired that he must carry her, and the shadows grow darker among the trees.
He sees pale shapes creeping through the wood and lights a fire to keep them away. The dry trees catch alight, and soon the whole forest is burning around them.
Smoke is everywhere, and in the confusion of the fight he feels Weena slip away from him. He searches and calls for her, but the fire is too fierce, and he can find no trace of her.
At dawn, he sits among the ashes, burned and dazed, and his grief is terrible. He has lost the only friend that he made in this strange world, and there is nothing that he can do.
At last, he drags himself back to the white sphinx, and to his surprise the bronze doors are standing open. He knows that it may be a trap, but he cannot leave his machine behind.
Inside the dark room, he finds his machine, and then the doors slam shut behind him. He lights a match, quickly puts the levers back in their place, and prepares to make his escape.
The Morlocks gather around him in the dark, and their cold hands reach out toward his face. He pulls the lever just in time, and the room, the creatures and the world around them fade away.
He travels onward for millions of years and stops at last on a lonely beach. The sun is huge and red, the sea is thick and still, and giant white crabs crawl slowly over the sand.
He goes even farther, to the very end of the Earth, where ice lies along the shore. The sun is almost dead and the air is bitterly cold, and the only living thing is a small round creature.
Feeling sick and cold, he turns the machine back toward his own time. Soon, the days and nights begin to flicker again, and the familiar walls of his laboratory appear around him.
When his story ends, the whole room is silent for a long moment. The guests look at him and at each other, and none of them knows what to say.

Some of the guests believe him, and some think that he is joking, and Filby says that it is a very good story. The Time Traveller laughs, but he looks tired, and he says that he has no real proof to show.
The next day, the narrator goes to the laboratory to ask more questions. He finds the Time Traveller packing a small bag and a camera, and he learns that he is going to make one more trip.
The Time Traveller promises to be back in half an hour. Before he goes, he shows the narrator two strange white flowers, which are unlike any flower that the narrator knows.
The Time Traveller walks out of the room, and the narrator waits for him, but he does not come back. An hour passes, then a day and then a week, and the machine stands quiet on the laboratory floor.
Three years go by, and the Time Traveller has still not returned, and no one has heard from him. Nobody knows whether he has been lost in time or has found a place to stay.
The narrator thinks about the world that the Time Traveller described, a world in which strong people prey on weak ones. He fears that, one day, it could be the real future of mankind.

Even so, he cannot believe that it must happen, because people can still learn and change. If we use our strength and our cleverness to care for one another, he hopes, we might build a different world.
On his desk lie the two white flowers, now dry and brown, that Weena once gave to the Time Traveller. They are the only proof that the story is true, and the narrator looks at them often.

The flowers remind him that even when strength and cleverness are lost, tenderness and gratitude may remain. With that thought, he closes the story, and he waits and hopes for the Time Traveller to return.
C1C2: On a winter evening, a circle of guests gathered at the Richmond house of the Time Traveller, a man whose restless curiosity was known to all his friends. The host himself had not yet appeared, so the company drifted toward the fire and talked idly of the weather and the news. Soon the door opened, and the conversation, which had been drowsy, began to wake.

With his usual gravity, the Time Traveller reminded them that every object in the world has length, breadth and thickness, but must also have a duration, since nothing can exist for no time at all. Time, he argued, was nothing but a fourth dimension, and the only reason men could not wander along it freely was the narrowness of human habit. A body could move in any direction of space, he said, so why should it not move up and down the stream of time?

The Psychologist objected that such an idea was a pretty paradox but impossible in practice, and Filby, always eager for an argument, added several objections of his own. The Time Traveller listened with his head on one side, smiling like a man who has a card up his sleeve and knows that the game is already his. At last, he declared that he could prove the whole thing with a model that stood in the next room.

He placed a small, glittering machine of nickel and ivory on the table, gave a lever a gentle push, and the model began to tremble and grow dim. Then, to the astonishment of everyone present, it dissolved into a faint blur and vanished, leaving only the lamplight and a puzzled silence. The Medical Man peered underneath the table, the Psychologist rubbed his eyes, and the Time Traveller calmly lit his pipe.

Afterward, some of the guests followed him down to the laboratory, where a larger version of the machine stood among his tools, shining with ivory, brass and crystal. It was unfinished, and some of its parts lay about on the bench, but even in that state it seemed to hum with a patient, secret power. Its maker said that he would soon sit upon it and ride into the past or the future, as he chose.

On the following Thursday, the guests returned as usual, but the Time Traveller was not at home, and the clock moved on toward eight with no sign of him. After some discussion, the company agreed to begin without their host and sat down to a dinner that was oddly quiet. An empty chair at the head of the table seemed to watch them all.

The door opened at last, and a figure staggered into the room whom they hardly recognized, with a dirty, pale face, a torn and dusty coat and a limp in his foot. He murmured that he was very sorry for his lateness and asked only for a little time to wash and to eat before he said anything. The narrator, who had known him for years, saw that his hair was streaked with gray, and that his eyes were bright with something that was not quite fear.

When he had been fed and rested, and the guests had made a half-circle around his chair, the Time Traveller began his tale in a low and level voice. That very morning, he told them, he had screwed the last parts of his machine into place and had been unable to wait one moment longer to try it. Nobody else had known of his intention, and he asked them to hear the account patiently, because he did not expect anyone to believe it.

As soon as he pushed the first lever, he felt a sensation of falling, and a dreadful sickness seized him, as if he were being dragged out of the world. The laboratory grew faint around him like smoke, and day and night began to alternate, flickering across his sight like the beating of a great black wing. He gripped the saddle of the machine and was surprised to find that he was not afraid, but only curious.

The sun leapt across the sky in a single bright streak, and the seasons passed in a blur of green and white, while buildings sprang up and sank back like frail bubbles. Giddy and frightened by the speed, he began to dread a collision with something solid, for he knew that he might arrive inside a wall or a rock. In panic, he seized the lever and hauled it back, and the world around him began to slow.

The machine reeled, and he was thrown headlong onto soft turf, while a savage hailstorm drove down upon him out of a heavy sky. Bruised and dazed, he scrambled to his feet, drenched and shivering, and looked about at a rolling country of hills, with the machine lying on its side behind him. It was the strangest moment of his life, and he knew that he had traveled far from home.

Through the driving rain, he saw dimly the figure of an enormous statue, white and shining, set on a pedestal of bronze and standing as high as a house. It was a sphinx, with a human face and a pair of wings that seemed half open, and he thought that the stone was ancient and the weather had bitten deep into it. Something in its blind gaze made him feel small, and he wondered who had carved it, and what had become of them.

As the hail eased, a number of small people came hurrying through the wet toward him, dressed in brightly colored robes, and he saw at once that they were beautiful. They were scarcely four feet tall, delicate in every feature, with curling hair and rosy faces, and they spoke to one another in soft, musical tones. There was no hostility in them, and no fear, and they gathered around the stranger as children gather around a visitor with a present.

They touched his sleeve, examined his strange clothes with wondering fingers and hung wreaths of flowers about his neck, laughing all the while as if they had known him for years. When he pointed to the sky to explain that he had come from above, they only laughed more, and he realized that they could neither follow his meaning nor believe it. He saw that they did not seem to wonder at him at all, which struck him as very odd.

He hurried back to the place where he had left his machine, and there he found nothing except the broad marks of its feet leading toward the pedestal of the sphinx. A cold horror rose in him, for without the machine he had no way to return, and he was stranded in a time he did not understand. He searched the bushes, called aloud, and at last sat down in despair, while the gentle people looked on in wonder.

For a time he made up his mind to stay among them, and by pointing at objects and repeating the words they spoke, he learned a few phrases of their simple tongue. It was slow work, for the little people soon grew tired of his questions and drifted away to play or sleep, as though nothing could hold their attention for long. Nevertheless, he gathered that the machine was not lost to the world, only hidden, and that there was a secret about the sphinx.

As he observed their way of life, he saw that they dwelt in great, ruined halls of stone and ate nothing but fruit, which they gathered from trees that grew everywhere. Every evening they lay down together in the large rooms and slept in heaps, as if they feared to be alone, and they seemed untroubled by anything except the dark. They had no books, no tools and no sign of any work, and the Time Traveller found this very strange.

At first, he thought that he understood them perfectly, and he explained to himself that mankind had grown soft in a world that required no labor and held no danger. Because the conflicts of earlier ages had ended, strength and cleverness had faded together, until only these pretty, idle creatures remained, living happily on the earth. He felt sad, but a little proud, to have seen the end of all human struggle, and it seemed to him that the story was told.

One warm afternoon, beside a bright river, one of the little women slipped from the bank into the current and began to drown, while her companions merely stood and watched. The Time Traveller, who was shocked at their indifference, plunged in and dragged her to the shore, and she lay gasping on the grass. The others thanked him politely and went back to their playing, as though a rescue were of no more consequence than a flower.

The woman he had saved was named Weena, and she attached herself to him at once, following him wherever he went with a trusting smile and stuffing his pockets with flowers. In her quiet, childlike way, she grew to be his dearest companion in that strange country, and he found that her presence made the days less lonely. Though she understood little of what he said, her gentle manners warmed him, and he began to love her as one loves a child.

But the nights unsettled him, for when darkness fell, the Eloi crowded together in terror, and he sometimes glimpsed pale, ghostly shapes sliding across the shadowy ground. They were swift and silent, with large, shining eyes, and they seemed to vanish into the earth wherever he turned to look. He began to suspect that the pleasant surface of this world was only a thin and fragile covering, and that something lay beneath it that he had not understood.

On his wanderings, he discovered a number of deep wells, round and dark, with no water in them, and from far down inside came a regular pulse of noise like the beating of great engines. A warm, stale draught breathed upward out of the darkness, and when he dropped a flower into one of them, it fell for a long time before he heard it land. He could hardly doubt that someone, or something, was at work below the ground.

His mind returned again and again to the machine, and he gradually formed a new theory, for he saw that the Eloi who lived in the sunlight could not possibly keep a world of machinery running by themselves. Someone else, he reasoned, must be tending the furnaces and the ventilating shafts, a different race that dwelt under the earth and never came up to the light. The notion made him uneasy, but he knew that he could not rest until he had seen for himself.

Taking a deep breath, he lowered himself into one of the wells, gripping the iron rungs that were fixed in the wall, and descended for what seemed an hour into a hot, humming blackness. When his feet touched solid ground at last, he struck a match and saw dimly a low tunnel, and moving in its shadow he saw pale, apelike creatures with huge, grey eyes. The creatures shrank from the light with soft cries, and they stared at him like creatures woken from sleep.

The Morlocks, as he would later call them, pressed in on him in the dark, their cold hands feeling at his clothes and face, and he realized that he was in great danger. His matches were nearly gone, but he lit another and drove them back for a moment, and he scrambled up the rungs with the creatures clutching at his heels. Not until he stood on the grass beneath the open sky did he stop to breathe, shaking with relief.

Slowly, a horrible truth dawned on him, for he understood at last what the little people feared, and why they huddled together as night approached. After sunset, the Morlocks climbed up out of the wells, hunting in the darkness, and they carried off the unwary Eloi to eat them in their caverns below. The gentle folk of the surface, he saw, were merely cattle, fed and fattened by the sun, and kept for the table of their masters.

He saw, at last, how the long story of mankind had ended, for he guessed that in earlier ages the rich had gradually shut themselves away from the poor, until the quarrel became a division of species. The idle masters had grown weak and pretty, while the toiling workers, living in the dark, had grown pale and savage, and in the end the roles had been reversed. The upper creatures were now the livestock of the lower, and he could feel no pleasure in the justice of it.

Reasoning further, he guessed that the Morlocks had hauled his machine into the pedestal of the sphinx, for the tracks in the grass led straight to its bronze doors. The doors were fastened tightly, and he could not force them, and he understood that the machine had been taken, not by accident, but because the creatures wished to understand it. If he wished to go home, he must first overcome his enemies, and that meant arming himself with something better than his bare hands.

He remembered a great ruined building that stood far away across the hills, a palace of greenish china, and he hoped that he might find weapons or tools among its ancient treasures. Taking Weena by the hand, he set out at dawn across the sunlit valleys, and she skipped beside him, picking flowers and chattering. It was a long journey, and it would take them most of the day to reach the palace.

The Palace of Green Porcelain turned out to be a vast and silent museum, filled with the rusty skeletons of machines, cases of broken glass and the dust of ages. Wandering through the gloom, the Time Traveller found a box of matches that had survived the centuries, a lump of camphor, which burns brightly, and a heavy iron bar to use as a weapon. He weighed the bar in his hand with grim satisfaction, for he felt like a man again.

Evening was already falling when they started back through a thick forest, and Weena, who had walked all day, grew so tired that he took her in his arms and carried her. Dark shadows fell between the trees, and he heard the whispering of soft feet and saw glimpses of white shapes moving at the corner of his eye. He quickened his pace, but his legs were heavy, and his heart sank at the thought of the long night that lay ahead.

Realizing that he could not go on, he lit a fire of dry branches and sat Weena down beside it, but the flames spread through the dry underbrush faster than he had expected. Soon the whole wood was blazing, with sparks flying overhead and the Morlocks dashing blindly through the glare, shrieking, and clutching at their eyes. The Time Traveller laid about him with the iron bar, striking at pale limbs as they came out of the smoke.

In the roaring, smoky confusion, he felt Weena's small hand slip from his own, and when he looked for her, she had vanished. He shouted her name, plunged through the burning bushes and searched until his eyes streamed, but nothing answered, and the heat drove him back. He never saw her again, and in the end he fell exhausted among the ashes, knowing that he had done everything and failed.

At dawn, the light crept over a blackened hillside strewn with the bodies of the Morlocks, and the Time Traveller lay among them, burned, bruised and lost in grief. He thought of Weena, so small and trusting, and of how she had followed him through a world that she did not fear until the night, and he wept without shame. Nothing more was left to him now except his machine, and the desperate hope of getting home.

At last, he rose, and with the iron bar in his hand, he walked back across the hills to the white sphinx, standing in the morning sun with its blind and patient face. To his surprise, the bronze doors were open, and the dark chamber inside was plainly visible, with something shining at the far end. He understood that it might be a trap, but he knew that he would go in regardless.

There, to his joy, stood his machine, and he ran to it and began to fit the levers back into their sockets, which the Morlocks had removed. Behind him, the bronze doors swung shut with a clang, and he was left in the dark among the pale creatures that had been waiting for him. He struck a match, his hands trembling, and the flame trembled with them as he worked.

The Morlocks pressed close, their cold fingers grasping at his coat, and he felt their soft breath on his face as he pushed the last lever into place. With a cry, he threw himself upon the machine and hauled the first lever forward, and the creatures, the chamber and the whole dark world slid away from him like a bad dream. He was moving through time once more, and for the moment nothing in the whole wide universe could catch him or do him any harm.

Thousands of years sped by, and then millions, until at last he drew the lever back and found himself beside a quiet sea, under a sun that was huge, red and dim. The beach was littered with strange plants, and over the sand crawled enormous white crabs, slowly turning their heavy claws as they looked for something to eat. The air was thin and still, and the sea moved sluggishly, as though the very waters were tired.

He traveled farther still, to the last age of the Earth, where ice gathered along the shore and the sun hung low, a dull and dying disc in a sky almost black. Nothing moved there but a single round, dark creature, hopping feebly across the sand, and the air was so cold that it hurt to breathe. At that moment, he felt a loneliness greater than any he had known, and he understood how small mankind was in the great scheme of things.

Sick and shaken, he turned the machine around and began the long journey back, watching the days flicker by until the walls of a familiar room grew solid around him. To his astonishment, he was in his own laboratory, with the same clock ticking on the wall and the same instruments lying on the bench. He climbed down from the saddle, brushed himself off and walked into the dining room where his friends were waiting.

His story ended, and for a long moment no one spoke, while the lamp burned low and the fire settled in the grate. The guests looked at the speaker with troubled faces, and some of them glanced at one another, unsure whether they had been told a wonderful truth or a very clever lie. The Time Traveller smiled wearily, and it seemed that he, too, was waiting for someone to say something.

Some of the company said that the Time Traveller must have been overworked, and the Mayor argued that it was a fine tale, though quite unbelievable, while Filby declared that he preferred it to any magazine story. The Time Traveller laughed and shrugged, for he had no evidence to show them except the dust upon his clothes and a small wound on his foot. He said that he would bring them proof, and he refused to say more.

The next day, the narrator, whose curiosity would not let him rest, called at the laboratory and found the Time Traveller at work, packing a small bag and a camera. The inventor explained that he intended to make one more journey, and that this time he would bring back evidence that no one could deny. In his pocket he carried a pair of strange white flowers, and he said that they came from the future.

He promised to return within half an hour, shook hands with the narrator and went out of the room, leaving the two white flowers lying on the bench. The narrator looked at them closely, for they were soft and curiously shaped, and he knew no plant like them in all of England. When he turned around, the machine seemed to waver in the lamplight, and then he was alone in the silent room.

He waited for what seemed an eternity, and the clock struck, and the sun climbed and fell, and still the Time Traveller did not come back. The machine stood where it had always stood, but now it was silent and cold, and the laboratory felt as empty as a tomb. Day after day, the narrator returned, hoping to find his friend sitting at his desk, but each time he was disappointed.

Three years have gone by since that day, and the Time Traveller has never reappeared, nor has any message come from him through the post or any other way. Friends have suggested that he may have been lost in some terrible gulf of time, or marooned in an age that he cannot leave. The narrator, who knows nothing for certain, can only keep his silent watch and go on wondering what became of him.

Sometimes the narrator fears that the future of man may be as dark as the Time Traveller described, a world in which comfort and cruelty have grown together until the human race divided against itself. In such moods, he sees the greed and carelessness of his own age as seeds from which that dreadful harvest might grow. Yet he cannot accept it, because the world has not yet been sealed in its course.

At other times he feels more hopeful, and in those hours he thinks that the Time Traveller's story may be a warning rather than a prophecy, a thing that may yet be avoided. Men have the power to change their habits, and if they will use their cleverness to look after one another, the dark dividing line might never be drawn. Only the years that lie ahead will show whether mankind rises to that great task.

On his writing table, in a small glass dish, lie the two white flowers that the Time Traveller left behind, now brown and brittle and withered with age. They are the single piece of evidence that the strange journey was real, and he looks at them often, thinking of the small, brave girl who gave them away. He cannot say for certain what became of the Time Traveller, but he can say that someone once cared enough to give a flower.

For the narrator, the flowers say that even when strength and cleverness have faded from the world, gratitude and tenderness may still be left in the human heart. That thought, he decides, is worth keeping, whatever the future holds and wherever the Time Traveller may be. With a quiet hope, he closes his book, and he leaves the lamp burning in the window in case his friend should return.
